title: MITRE ATT&CK & the Kill Chain
summary: The map of attacker behavior used by security teams worldwide.

pages.title: The Cyber Kill Chain
pages.body:
The kill chain breaks an attack into ordered stages:
1. Reconnaissance: researching the target (LV.04)
2. Weaponization: preparing tools, e.g. a malware-laden document
3. Delivery: sending it, e.g. via phishing email
4. Exploitation: a flaw is used
5. Installation: malware persists
6. Command & Control: the attacker controls it remotely
7. Actions on objectives: stealing data, encrypting, etc.

The lesson: defenses can break the chain at any stage. The earlier it breaks, the smaller the damage.
pages.tip: Like a bicycle chain: break one link and the bike stops.

pages.title: MITRE ATT&CK
pages.body:
MITRE ATT&CK is an open knowledge base of real attacker behavior, organized as a matrix:
- Tactics: the attacker's goals, e.g. Initial Access, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Exfiltration
- Techniques: how they achieve them, e.g. Phishing (T1566) or Valid Accounts (T1078)

Security teams use it to:
- Map which detections exist and which are missing
- Speak a shared language when reporting incidents
- Design red team and purple team exercises

All of ATT&CK is free at attack.mitre.org.
pages.tip: ATT&CK is like the attackers' complete cookbook. Defenders read it so they know which dishes are coming.

pages.title: Applying it
pages.body:
Example: the APK invitation scam from LV.05 can be mapped:
- Initial Access: phishing via a chat app
- Execution: the victim installs the APK
- Credential Access: reading OTP SMS
- Exfiltration: sending data to a Telegram bot

Once mapped, the team asks at each stage: "what could detect or block this?". For example user education early on, Play Protect at execution, and bank transaction monitoring at the end.
pages.tip: Mapping an attack is like drawing the burglar's route, then putting CCTV at every turn.

quiz.prompt: The core idea of the kill chain is...
options: Attacks have stages; breaking one can foil the whole attack
quiz.explanation: The earlier it breaks, the smaller the damage.

quiz.prompt: In MITRE ATT&CK, "Persistence" is a...
quiz.explanation: Tactic = goal, technique = method.

quiz.prompt: ATT&CK's use for blue teams is...
quiz.explanation: It helps prioritize defenses.

quiz.prompt: The stage of sending stolen data out is called...
quiz.explanation: Exfiltration = data leaving the victim's network.

quiz.prompt: The earliest kill chain stage is...
quiz.explanation: Researching the target always comes first.

title: Threat Hunting & Detection
summary: Hunting attackers who slipped past alarms, and writing your own detection rules.

pages.title: Don't wait for alarms
pages.body:
Threat hunting is actively searching for attacker traces, assuming "someone may already be in but undetected". Hunters start from a hypothesis, e.g.:
- "If stolen passwords are in use, there'll be successful logins from unusual countries"
- "If malware persisted, there'll be odd new scheduled tasks"

Then they test the hypothesis against log data. Confirmed findings become automated detection rules.
pages.tip: A regular guard waits for the alarm. A hunter walks around checking windows that look shut but aren't locked.

pages.title: Detection rules: Sigma
pages.body:
Sigma is an open detection rule format, like a "recipe" translatable to many SIEMs. A simple example detecting many failed Windows logins:
| title: Many failed logins
| logsource:
|   product: windows
|   service: security
| detection:
|   selection:
|     EventID: 4625
|   condition: selection | count() > 20
| level: medium

The community shares thousands of free Sigma rules, many mapped to ATT&CK techniques.
pages.tip: A detection rule is like a wanted poster at the guard post: anyone matching gets flagged.

pages.title: Detection quality
pages.body:
Good detection rules are balanced:
- Too loose: lots of false positives, the team burns out and starts ignoring alerts (recall LV.06)
- Too strict: attackers who vary slightly slip through (false negatives)

Healthy practice:
- Test rules with simulated attack data (purple teaming)
- Document why each alert matters and how to respond (playbooks)
- Measure: time from event to detection, and to resolution

Practice: TryHackMe's SOC Level 1 path covers log analysis and detection.
pages.tip: An alarm that rings for every passing cat gets unplugged. An alarm that never rings is useless too.

quiz.prompt: Threat hunting starts from...
quiz.explanation: The hypothesis is then tested against data.

quiz.prompt: Sigma is...
options: An open detection rule format translatable to many SIEMs
quiz.explanation: One rule, many platforms.

quiz.prompt: An overly loose detection rule causes...
quiz.explanation: False alarms make teams careless.

quiz.prompt: A false negative means...
options: An alarm on a safe event
A real attack that went undetected
quiz.explanation: This is the most dangerous kind.

quiz.prompt: Purple teaming is...
options: Red and blue teams working together to test detections
quiz.explanation: Simulated attacks are used to improve detection.

title: Malware Analysis
summary: Dissecting malware safely: static, dynamic, and YARA.

pages.title: Safe lab first
pages.body:
Malware analysis must happen in an isolated environment:
- A dedicated virtual machine with snapshots so it can be reverted
- Network disconnected or redirected to a fake network
- No personal accounts, important files, or folders shared with the main computer
- Samples kept in password-protected archives (by convention the password "infected") so they aren't run by accident

A mistake here can infect your own computer.
pages.tip: Malware analysis is like studying viruses in a biosafety lab: sealed doors, special suits, nothing goes home.

pages.title: Static vs dynamic
pages.body:
Static analysis (without running it):
- Hash the file and look it up on VirusTotal
- Read embedded strings: URLs, IPs, file names, messages
- Inspect headers, libraries used, and permissions (like the APK dissection in LV.08)
- Decompile or disassemble with tools like Ghidra (free, from the NSA) for Windows/Linux programs

Dynamic analysis (run in a sandbox):
- Watch processes created, files changed, registry edits, and network connections
- Online sandboxes like ANY.RUN or Hybrid Analysis show its behavior

The output is Indicators of Compromise (IoCs): hashes, domains, IPs, file names other teams can use for detection.
pages.tip: Static is reading the recipe without cooking. Dynamic is cooking in a sealed kitchen while watching where the smoke goes.

pages.title: YARA: malware fingerprints
pages.body:
YARA is a rule language for recognizing files by patterns. An example detecting scam APKs that send data to a Telegram bot:
| rule APK_Telegram_Exfil {
|   strings:
|     $a = "api.telegram.org/bot"
|     $b = "android.permission.RECEIVE_SMS"
|   condition:
|     all of them
| }

YARA rules are used by antivirus engines, sandboxes, and incident response teams to scan thousands of files at once. They're written from analysis findings, then shared with the community.
pages.tip: YARA is like a wanted photo sent to every post: the moment something matches, it's caught.

quiz.prompt: Malware analysis should be done on...
quiz.explanation: Isolation prevents infection from spreading.

quiz.prompt: Static analysis means...
options: Examining the file without running it
quiz.explanation: Reading strings, headers, and code.

quiz.prompt: Examples of Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)...
options: Malicious file hashes, domains, and IPs
quiz.explanation: IoCs are used for detection elsewhere.

quiz.prompt: Ghidra is...
quiz.explanation: Released open-source by the NSA.

quiz.prompt: YARA is used to...
quiz.explanation: YARA rules scan many files at once.

title: Large-Scale Incident Response
summary: When ransomware hits the office: decisions, communication, and recovery.

pages.title: The first hours
pages.body:
Scenario: Monday morning, dozens of office computers show a ransom note. First-hour decisions are critical:
- Isolate: disconnect affected devices from the network, but don't power them off yet (evidence in memory may be lost)
- Protect backups: make sure they're disconnected and not encrypted too
- Activate the response team and chain of command: who decides what
- Record everything with timestamps (a timeline) from the first minute

Panic makes people delete evidence or shut down the wrong servers. That's what a rehearsed plan is for.
pages.tip: Like a building fire: close doors so it doesn't spread, save key documents, and follow the evacuation route you practiced.

pages.title: Communication & obligations
pages.body:
A major incident isn't just technical:
- Internal: staff need to know what to do and not do; don't coordinate over email that may be compromised
- Leadership: needs the business impact, not technical detail
- Customers and the public: honest, timely communication
- Regulators: data protection laws often require prompt notification; Indonesia's PDP Law requires written notice within 3 x 24 hours of a personal data protection failure
- Law enforcement and relevant agencies

Whether to pay a ransom involves leadership, legal, and often insurers.
pages.tip: When your house is burgled, you don't just fix the door. You tell the family, report it, and handle the insurance.

pages.title: Recover and learn
pages.body:
Proper recovery:
- Make sure the attacker's access is truly gone (accounts, backdoors, persistence) before restoring; otherwise the attack can repeat
- Restore from clean backups, critical systems first
- Rotate every credential that may have leaked
- Monitor closely for weeks afterwards

Then run a blameless post-incident review: what happened, why it was possible, what gets fixed. Rehearse the plan with tabletop exercises: discussion-based "what if..." simulations with the team and leadership.
pages.tip: Before moving back into a burned house, make sure every ember is out.

quiz.prompt: When ransomware is detected, affected devices should be...
options: Isolated from the network without powering off yet
quiz.explanation: Evidence in memory may be lost if powered off.

quiz.prompt: Why avoid coordinating an incident over office email?
quiz.explanation: The attacker could read the response plan.

quiz.prompt: Indonesia's PDP Law requires notifying a data protection failure within...
quiz.explanation: Written notice to data subjects and the authority.

quiz.prompt: Before restoring from backup, you must ensure...
options: The attacker's access is truly removed
quiz.explanation: Otherwise the attack can repeat.

quiz.prompt: A tabletop exercise is...
options: A discussion-based "what if" simulation to rehearse the response plan
quiz.explanation: It rehearses decisions without waiting for a real incident.
